cases.question: Why was March 2018 so bad for deliveries?
cases.headline: March 2018 was genuinely elevated: 19.0% of delivered orders were late versus a 5.8% baseline, with the gap concentrated in carrier transit time.
notes: Late rate was 19.0% against a 5.8% baseline, a gap of 13.2 percentage points, across 7,003 delivered orders (1,328 late).

Transit days averaged 12.97 versus a 9.06-day baseline, about 3.9 days longer, while handling days were close to baseline (3.33 vs 3.19) and promised days were slightly shorter than baseline (22.03 vs 23.78).
The pattern was systemic rather than confined to a few states: the late rate excluding the top two states was still 23.7%.
RJ stood out with a 34.5% late rate versus a 10.5% baseline (864 orders, 208 excess late orders), followed by SP at 9.4% versus 4.1% and MG at 20.4% versus 3.3%.
Late orders were associated with much lower review scores (2.07 vs 4.21) and a 59.3% one-star share versus 7.9% for on-time orders.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Late orders were spread across 466 sellers, with the top five accounting for only 11.5% of them, so no single seller explains the period.
Some category samples are small, such as audio with 33 orders, so those rates are less reliable.

cases.question: What went wrong with deliveries in February 2018?
cases.headline: February 2018 deliveries ran late at more than double the baseline rate, with the excess concentrated in carrier transit time and in the state of RJ.
notes: The late rate was 14.1% versus a 6.3% baseline, a gap of 7.8 percentage points, across 6,555 delivered orders (926 late).
Carrier transit was the top driver: transit averaged 13.38 days against a 9.05-day baseline, roughly 4.3 days longer, while handling was 3.56 versus 3.18 days.
RJ stood out with a 34.0% late rate versus a 10.5% baseline (879 orders, 207 excess late orders); SP (7.3% vs 4.3%) and SC (24.0% vs 7.0%) also ran above baseline.

The pattern was systemic rather than confined to a few states: the late rate excluding the top two states was 14.3%, and late orders spanned 357 sellers with the top five accounting for 13.9% of them.
Late deliveries coincided with much lower reviews: average review 1.91 versus 4.2 on time, and 64.1% one-star reviews versus 7.7% on time.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category figures are shown without excess late order counts, and some category samples are small (for example construction_tools_construction at 53 orders).
The findings describe associations only and do not establish causes.

notes: Late rate was 12.4% versus a 6.3% baseline, a gap of 6.1 percentage points across 7,288 delivered orders (904 late).

The pattern was systemic: excluding the two worst states, the late rate was still 13.0%.
RJ stood out with a 26.0% late rate versus a 10.9% baseline (1,012 orders, 153 excess late orders); SP and RS were also above baseline.
Late deliveries coincided with much lower reviews: 2.2 average versus 4.24 on time, and 55.9% one-star share versus 7.1%.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category figures rest on small samples (for example 40 orders for home_confort, 37 for books_general_interest).

cases.question: Investigate late deliveries to Minas Gerais in March 2018.
cases.headline: Late deliveries to Minas Gerais in March 2018 were elevated: 20.4% of the 856 delivered orders arrived late versus a 3.3% baseline, a gap of about 17.1 percentage points.
notes: The verdict is elevated: 175 of 856 delivered orders were late (20.4%), compared with a baseline rate of 3.3%.
The top driver was carrier_transit: transit took 13.19 days versus a baseline of 8.43 days, roughly 4.8 days longer.
Handling time was only slightly longer than baseline (3.57 versus 3.18 days), while the promised window was actually shorter than baseline (22.49 versus 24.62 days).
Lateness was concentrated in a few categories: bed_bath_table (83 orders, 34.9% late vs 4.3% baseline), health_beauty (79 orders, 27.8% vs 2.2%), and housewares (41 orders, 26.8% vs 2.2%).
Late orders were associated with much lower review scores (2.15 vs 4.08 on time) and a higher share of one-star reviews (58.3% vs 9.4%).
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Lateness was spread across many sellers: 118 sellers had late orders, and the top 5 sellers accounted for only 16.6% of them.
Review figures cover 168 late and 679 on-time orders, so the review comparison rests on a smaller late-order sample.

cases.question: Why did late deliveries rise in December 2017?
cases.headline: December 2017 was not unusual: the late rate of 7.5% was only 0.8 points above the 6.7% baseline, so the period does not stand out as a late-delivery problem.
notes: Late orders were 411 of 5,513 delivered orders (7.5%), versus a 6.7% baseline, a gap of 0.8 percentage points.
The excess was concentrated in RJ: 746 orders at a 24.0% late rate against an 11.4% baseline, about 94 excess late orders; RS (10.1% vs 5.9%) and PR (5.0% vs 4.0%) were much smaller contributors.
Excluding the top two states, the late rate was 4.5%, below the overall 7.5% and the 6.7% baseline.
Handling averaged 3.72 days versus a 3.17-day baseline and transit 11.67 days versus 9.2 days, roughly 0.6 and 2.5 days longer respectively; promised days were also longer (27.68 vs 23.4).
Late orders coincided with lower reviews (2.11 vs 4.24) and a higher one-star share (58.4% vs 7.0%).
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category findings rest on small samples (musical_instruments n=41, office_furniture n=38), and no excess-late-order counts are given for categories.
Late orders were spread across 195 sellers, with the top 5 accounting for only 17.3%, so no single seller explains the period.

cases.question: Why did review scores drop in March 2018?
cases.headline: March 2018 review scores were unusually low, averaging 3.75 versus a 4.11 baseline, with the one-star share nearly doubling to 19.0% from 10.9%.
notes: The drop was concentrated in late deliveries: 56.6% of one-star reviews came from late orders, and late delivery contributed 7.8 of the 8.1-point rise in one-star share.
On-time orders contributed only 0.3 points and not-delivered orders roughly zero, so the shift was not spread evenly across delivery outcomes.
Among categories, audio (2.94 vs 3.92 baseline, n=33), construction tools (3.36 vs 4.11, n=51), and toys (3.63 vs 4.19, n=221) scored lowest.
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Several category and seller samples are small (n=32 to n=51), so their scores are less stable.
Seller-level findings may reflect multi-seller attribution rather than a single seller's performance.
warnings_at_run: The narration uses causal wording (cause); the data shows associations only.

cases.question: What caused the low review scores in February 2018?
cases.headline: February 2018 review scores were below baseline, with late delivery the top associated driver.
notes: Average score was 3.83 versus a baseline of 4.11, and the one-star share was 17.1% versus 11.0% (a 6.1 point gap).
Late delivery was the top driver, contributing 5.7 of the 6.1 point one-star gap; on-time contributed 0.5 and not-delivered -0.1.
Among one-star reviews, 51.2% came from late orders, 37.9% from on-time orders, and 10.9% from not-delivered orders.
The weakest category by score was computers_accessories (3.45 vs 4.0 baseline, n=795), followed by luggage_accessories (3.5 vs 4.35, n=44) and food (3.67 vs 4.26, n=31).
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Some category and seller samples are small (e.g., luggage_accessories n=44, food n=31, sellers n=32-49), so their scores are less stable.
Seller-level findings may reflect multi-seller attribution rather than a single seller's performance.
warnings_at_run: The narration uses causal wording (cause); the data shows associations only.

cases.headline: Reviews in Rio de Janeiro in March 2018 were unusually low, with an average score of 3.18 versus a 3.93 baseline and a one-star share of 33.5% versus 15.7%.
notes: The one-star share was 17.8 percentage points above baseline, and late delivery was the top driver.

Late delivery contributed 17.1 points to the one-star share, while on-time contributed 0.1 points and not-delivered 0.6 points.
The lowest-scoring categories were electronics (2.92 vs 3.86 baseline, n=45), sports_leisure (3.01 vs 3.91, n=77), and watches_gifts (2.95 vs 3.82, n=59).
No worst sellers were identified in the findings.
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Category samples are small (n=45 to 77), so those category-level scores are less reliable.
The findings do not attribute issues to individual sellers, so multi-seller effects cannot be separated.

cases.question: Why were deliveries so bad in July 2017?
cases.headline: July 2017 was not a bad month for deliveries: the late rate was 2.8%, well below the 7.0% baseline.
notes: Late deliveries came in at 2.8% of 3,872 delivered orders, 4.2 percentage points below the 7.0% baseline.
Handling and transit times were both slightly faster than baseline: 3.11 versus 3.21 days handling, and 8.51 versus 9.38 days in transit (about 0.9 days shorter).
The states with the most late orders (SC, PR, RS) all ran below their own baselines, with negative excess late orders.
Late orders were associated with much lower review scores: 2.25 average versus 4.32 for on-time orders, and 54.3% of late orders drew one-star reviews versus 5.5% of on-time orders.
Late orders were spread across 83 sellers, with the top five accounting for 19.4% of them, so no single seller stands out.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category-level counts are small (45 to 80 orders), so those rates are noisy.
The review comparison is an association, not evidence that lateness produced the lower scores.

cases.question: Investigate the late deliveries in June 2018.

Late orders were associated with much lower review scores (2.31 vs 4.33) and a higher one-star share (52.1% vs 6.6%).
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Late orders were spread across 58 sellers, with the top 5 accounting for only 16.9% of them, so no single seller explains the pattern.
Category-level samples are small (for example, drinks n=30, consoles_games n=41), limiting how much can be read into those rates.

followups.question: Which 5 sellers had the most late orders?
followups.sql: WITH late_by_seller AS (SELECT oi.seller_id, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS late_orders FROM analytics.order_items AS oi JOIN analytics.orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE o.is_delivered AND o.is_late AND o.purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) GROUP BY oi.seller_id) SELECT seller_id, late_orders FROM late_by_seller ORDER BY late_orders DESC, seller_id LIMIT 5
followups.headline: The seller 4869f7a5dfa277a7dca6462dcf3b52b2 had the most late orders in March 2018, with 35.

followups.question: How many late orders were there?
followups.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS late_orders FROM analytics.orders WHERE is_delivered AND is_late AND purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) AND customer_state = 'RJ' LIMIT 501
followups.headline: There were 298 late orders in the applied scope.

followups.question: What was the average carrier transit time in days?
followups.sql: SELECT ROUND(CAST(AVG(carrier_transit_days) AS DECIMAL), 2) AS avg_carrier_transit_days FROM analytics.orders WHERE purchase_month = CAST('2018-02-01' AS DATE) AND is_delivered = TRUE AND carrier_transit_days IS NOT NULL LIMIT 501
followups.headline: The average carrier transit time for delivered orders purchased in February 2018 was 13.38 days.

followups.question: How many orders were delivered?
followups.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders FROM analytics.orders WHERE is_delivered = TRUE AND purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) AND customer_state = 'MG' LIMIT 501
followups.headline: 856 orders were delivered.

followups.question: What share of reviews were 1-star?
followups.sql: SELECT ROUND(CAST(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE review_score = 1) / COUNT(*) AS DECIMAL), 2) AS one_star_share_pct FROM analytics.orders WHERE purchase_month = CAST('2018-03-01' AS DATE) AND review_score IS NOT NULL LIMIT 501
followups.headline: About 19% of reviewed orders in March 2018 received a 1-star review.
